title: Kacha, the student in the enemy's house
hookLine: a god's son studies under the asuras' teacher, and the handbook on power bows to both
carry: before you begin, bow to your teachers
tomorrow: how many sciences does a ruler need? the old schools couldn't agree.
last: WHEN THE BOOK IS SILENT, LOOK TO THE GOOD.

lines: THE ENEMY'S TEACHER KNOWS THE MANTRA OF LIFE.
HE ANSWERS FROM INSIDE HIS TEACHER.
cards: The gods and the asuras are at war, and the asuras have a secret. Their teacher, Shukra, knows a mantra that brings the dead back to life. So the gods send a student.
Kacha, son of Brihaspati, the gods' own teacher, walks into the enemy's school and asks Shukra to teach him. Shukra takes him in. The asuras are furious.
They kill Kacha again and again, and each time, at the pleading of Shukra's daughter Devayani, Shukra calls him back. At last they burn him, mix the ashes into Shukra's wine, and Shukra drinks it.
Then Shukra calls his student's name, and Kacha answers from inside him.

teach.b: Now Shukra is stuck: to free his student, he has to die. So he teaches Kacha the mantra right there. Kacha bursts out, Shukra falls, and Kacha, newly taught, brings his teacher back to life.
The Mahabharata tells it in its first book: a student of the gods, honoring the asuras' teacher as his own. Hold that pair, Brihaspati and Shukra.

teach.h: FIRST LINE: A BOW TO BOTH TEACHERS.
teach.b: Open the Arthashastra, the old Sanskrit science of artha, wealth and statecraft, and they're both in its first line: a salutation to Shukra and Brihaspati, the teachers of both sides.
Then it says, in paraphrase, that it's gathered, for the most part, from the treatises earlier teachers wrote on gaining and protecting the earth.
That opening is a real Hindu habit with a name: mangalacharana, the auspicious beginning. Sanskrit works open with a bow, to a god or to the teachers, before a word of their own.
It's the same instinct that has students touch a teacher's feet, and keeps Guru Purnima, the day for honoring teachers. Learning, in this tradition, is received, never just taken.

Even a handbook on power says whose shoulders it stands on, rivals included. And artha isn't a word to blush at here. It's one of the aims of life, worth a whole science, and that science starts with a bow.

how: Many Hindu students begin study by touching a teacher's feet or praying to Saraswati, families honor teachers on Guru Purnima, and Sanskrit works traditionally open with a mangalacharana, a salutation, before their first word.

it opens with a bow, and says it's gathered from earlier teachers' treatises.
it salutes the teachers of both gods and asuras
Brihaspati and Shukra: the old rivals' teachers, side by side in the first line.
Kacha stole the mantra of life from Shukra's books
Shukra taught it to him, from inside his own body, so his student could bring him back.

games.q: your little cousin starts music lessons with a guru tomorrow and asks what to do first. by the Arthashastra's first line, what's the hindu way to begin?
o: bow to the teacher before the first note, and thank the ones it comes from.
play your best piece first, so the teacher sees what you've got.
skip the formalities. lessons are just a service you pay for.
games.why: hindu learning starts with a bow: mangalacharana in the books, touching a teacher's feet in the music room. even the handbook on power opens that way.

practice: Many Hindus begin study with a bow to the teacher, or a short prayer to Saraswati or Ganesha. If you pray, fold your hands and bow silently to one teacher before your next task.
If you don't, count slowly on your fingers the people your own work rests on, and give each one a breath.

wordCard.voice: The Arthashastra's opening: a mangalacharana, a bow to Shukra and Brihaspati, rival teachers side by side.

carryVoice: Your line: before you begin, bow to your teachers. Kacha did, in the enemy's house. Until tomorrow.
